ratings.text:
No hidden motive;
mean what you say.
ratings.reasons: Passes the rules: 17 and 18 characters (line 2 at the limit), 7 words, plain words, nothing oracular. It asks two things of the viewer and they are different things: line 1 is the open centre (line 1 of 61, 有它不燕: having another aim brings no peace), line 2 is the firm lines holding each trigram's centre, read as Wang Bi's 直而正 (straight and upright): your words match what is inside. A newcomer gets what 中孚 asks without knowing the name. It fits the picture: as the two yin halves slide apart the viewer sees that the centre is empty, nothing hidden there, which is line 1 said literally; it no longer claims the core is firm. No repeat: 29 is 'keep your word' (promise-keeping under danger), 25 is 'do what's right, not what pays' (motive of gain), 16 and 31 are influence; 'motive' and 'mean what you say' appear in no other lesson. Why not higher: line 2 has no visible counterpart, since the brightening of lines 2 and 5 reads as emphasis, not as speech, so the picture carries line 1 only. 'Hidden motive' has a faint suspicious, crime-drama tone that is stronger than 有它 (another aim). 'Mean what you say' is a stock idiom, and 1's meaning card already says 'Just mean it'. Line 1 is a verbless phrase and line 2 an imperative, so the grammar is mixed, though the semicolon holds them together. None of these justify a redo; alternatives tried in rounds 6 and 7 ('open at the heart', 'stand by your word', 'hold no agenda; keep your word') were weaker or repeated 29.
